children: Older Americans are less confident about managing their future finances than they are about handling today's money matters. That is according to a new study by pollster Gallup and wealth management company Edward Jones.

The study found that 54% of baby boomers expressed a great deal of confidence in their ability to manage their current financial needs. That was far higher than Gen Z adults at 25%, millennials at 31%, and Gen Xers at 38%.

Boomers' confidence diminishes, however, when it comes to future financial needs, with just 37% expressing surety that they can handle them. For Gen Z and millennial adults, the comparable figures are 26% and 25%, respectively. For Gen Xers, the figure is 26%.

Gallup's study interviewed more than 5,000 U.S. adults in March and April. The same study also interviewed more than 2,000 Canadian adults, and found a similar trend of greater confidence in handling today's financial needs than future ones.

Gen Xers are nearing retirement age, and their uncertainty about their ability to manage future finances may be a reflection of the current state of their retirement savings: Among Gen Xers in the U.S., 39% worry about whether their current and future savings will last, according to the study. (The figure is slightly higher in Canada, at 44%.) Fifty-nine percent of U.S. Gen Xers without a retirement plan express concerns about savings compared with 25% of those who have a retirement plan.
June data from Fidelity Investments show the average 401(k) and IRA balances for Gen Xers are $215,600 and $118,700, respectively. Fidelity is one of the nation's largest retirement plan providers.

Asset manager Schroders released additional findings from its 2026 U.S. Retirement Survey, which showed signs of retirement planning stress among investors. A majority, 52%, of nonretired Americans are concerned or very concerned about outliving their retirement savings, according to Schroders' survey. Nonretired Americans believe they will need $5,094 in monthly income to retire comfortably. Many aren't sure they have the ability to set aside enough savings to meet their needs. Just under half, 48%, say they are concerned AI will force them into retirement sooner than planned, according to Schroders' survey.

Priorities. The Gallup study shows that Gen X adults are far more likely than Gen Z adults to prioritize saving for retirement (62% versus 39%), which may not be too surprising given that Gen Xers are closer to retirement than their younger peers.

When asked about their financial priorities, all four generations ranked "having income for a healthy lifestyle" near the top of their list. Gen Z and millennial adults placed greater emphasis on saving to purchase a house than Gen X and baby boomer adults. Younger generations were also more likely to report feeling financial stress than older generations. One-third of Gen Z adults say they are working more hours than they would like to increase their income, compared with 24% and 23% of Gen X adults, respectively, Gallup's study says.

"Younger adults are focused on building the income and assets needed to reach milestones, and many are absorbing the cost of that effort through longer hours and more frequent financial stress," the study says. "For older adults, the challenge shifts from accumulating wealth to determining whether it will provide lasting financial security."
